entry.title: What's New on developers.sap.com Labor Day Edition
entry.content:
It's a long Labor Day weekend here in the US and Canada, but it's still been a genuinely busy stretch for developers.sap.com. Between the end of August and today we shipped four releases to production, and while plenty of it is plumbing you'll never notice, a lot of it is stuff you'll run into the moment you open a tutorial, the homepage, or the new Channels area. Grab a coffee, there's a lot to cover.

Hands-free navigation, and quieter accessibility wins

We've been building out webcam-based navigation for a while, and it took a real step forward. If you enable it, hand swipes now move you cleanly between the steps of a tutorial. Previously a swipe could misfire onto the Prev/Next pills and bounce you into an entirely different tutorial, which was maddening; that's fixed, and swipes at the first or last step simply do nothing. Eye-scrolling switched from tracking your iris to reading your head pitch, which turns out to be far more reliable: tilt your head down and the page scrolls down, tilt up and it scrolls up, with a comfortable neutral zone in the middle so you're not fighting it. Because everyone holds their head a little differently, there's now an optional five-second Calibrate step (plus a one-time prompt the first time you start) that builds a personal profile, so the tracking actually fits you. All of this runs entirely in your browser. Nothing about your camera ever touches a server.

Camera Controlled Eye-Tracking and Hand-Guestures

Alongside the flashy stuff, we did a quieter round of accessibility repairs: cleaning up duplicate page landmarks on the browse, advocates, and tutorial pages, wrapping the concepts pages in a proper main landmark, and darkening the tutorial figure-caption text so it comfortably clears the contrast standard. To keep any of that from silently regressing, every deploy now runs an automated accessibility scan that fails the release if something slips backward.

Tutorials that actually render and grade the way they should

A cluster of fixes landed that you'll feel as "things just look right now." A parser bug meant that any fenced code block indented with exactly four spaces, which happens constantly inside numbered steps, rendered its raw triple-backtick delimiters as visible text instead of a proper syntax-highlighted code window. That affected 469 tutorials. A follow-up fixed the related problem where the prose and screenshots that came after those blocks (the "your source code should now look like this" line and the screenshot under it) were getting swallowed inside the code block as literal text. On one ABAP RAP tutorial alone, that took literal-text code blocks from six down to zero and rendered images from 21 up to 30. A couple more fixes in the same family handle authors who disable a section by wrapping it in an HTML comment, that used to blank out the entire tutorial's steps and leave a stray -->on the page, and now it's handled cleanly.

We are always looking for things that don't quite render right. We have been authoring tutorials in markdown for more than 10 years with three different parser versions. So there are inevitable some quirks still out there, but fill in feedback or open a GitHub issue if you find anything and we'll get it fixed.

Quizzes got more trustworthy too. If a tutorial author wrote a yes/no question, the options were rendering on the page as the literal words "true" and "false," and — worse — a yes correct answer was being silently flipped so that grading of the text answer broke. Yes/no (and on/off, y/n) options and answers now stay exactly as intended. And for the AI-graded coding tutorials, the grader used to be too strict: it would fail perfectly correct learner code for leaving out details the goal never actually asked for. The concrete example was failing a title : localized String answer just because it omitted the (111) length that happened to be in the hidden reference solution. Now the goal is the whole rubric; the reference is treated as the floor for grading, not the ceiling, so you won't get dinged for a detail that was never part of the ask. Amazingly this was all because of a difference in YAML 1.1 and 1.2.

We also turned dead attachment links into real downloads. Tutorials that link to a bundled file (a .txt, .zip, .pdf, .csv, and so on) used to 404 on those links (44 of them, across 24 tutorials). Now those files are served properly: each gets a working inline-view link plus a download sibling, so text opens in the browser and binaries download. And for safety, .html attachments are served as plain text rather than executed. All these are stored alongside the SAP HANA Database in the SAP BTP Object Store.

A big new thing: Channels

This is probably the largest brand-new feature of the last two weeks. We pulled together a catalog of 238 SAP developer channels: YouTube shows, blogs, podcasts, community feeds, the lot. We built a whole little neighborhood of the site around them.

It starts at /channels, a searchable, filterable directory where you can slice by category, platform, and owner scope, with community-run channels clearly badged so you always know what's official and what's community. But it grew into more than a list. There's now a Channels Hub on top, with a few destinations worth knowing.

Channels Overview

Ecosystem Health (/channels/health) gives you a bird's-eye view of the whole landscap: counts by category, by status, by who runs each channel, with summary tiles.

Build Your Media Diet (/channels/media-diet) is the fun one: pick up to three focus areas and it hands you a ranked, curated set of up to a dozen channels to follow. If you're signed in, it can go further and recommend channels based on the tutorials you've actually completed, walking from your completions to their tags to matching, curator-reviewed channels. Once you've got a set you like, you can export it as an OPML file, browser bookmarks, or JSON, so it drops straight into your RSS reader or browser.

Media Diet

For the visually inclined there's the Channel Atlas at /channels/atlas. This is an interactive force-directed graph of the entire ecosystem. Each channel is a node, edges connect channels that share focus areas or topics, node size reflects reach (subscribers or GitHub stars), and colors group them by owner type, with a filter and a detail panel for each one. Every channel also got its own detail page, and we started stitching channels into the rest of the site: topic pages now carry a Related channels band pointing you to up to five curator-reviewed feeds relevant to whatever you're reading about.

Channel Atlas

And because a catalog like this only stays good if people tend it, signed-in users can now suggest a channel (add, edit, or flag one for removal) through a submission form, and those suggestions flow into a moderation queue for the team to review and apply.

Suggestion Box

Getting around

Finding your way around got noticeably better. The top navigation menu was rebuilt as a clean two-level, single-open menu grouped into Learn, Explore, and Community, and it finally includes the places people kept struggling to find or that weren't previously ready for prime time like: Channels, Topics, Browse, What's New, the App Space, the Tutorial Navigator, and Concepts all have proper homes now.

New Navigation

The menu and the ⌘K command palette read from a single shared source, so they can never drift out of sync, and both now carry a "Knowledge Graph" entry pointing at the interactive Explorer plus an "About the Knowledge Graph" entry explaining what it is and how it's built.

The Topics area got a real overhaul. It's now a proper drill-in tree. You can navigate from a broad facet down through folders to something specific like SAP HANA Cloud → Data Lake, instead of the old flat list where every entry just showed its whole path as one leaf. Each topic has its own page with related concepts pulled in automatically. And on tutorial pages, the tags in the Overview section are finally clickable. Tap one and you'll see every tutorial that shares it, exactly like the header chips already did.

Topics Tree

The Tutorial Navigator got some love too. Its Featured Missions cards, which had been rendering completely blank since go live thanks to a nasty bug (empty title, empty description, "0 min) now show real titles, descriptions, levels, times, and tags. And the whole page no longer lurches on load: the hero, search, filters, and toolbar used to pop in a beat late and shove the first card hundreds of pixels down the screen, and now the full chrome is server-rendered so the grid sits in its final position from the very first paint.

Featured Missions

Admins didn't get left out. The admin console now has its own command palette (the search icon in the header, or Ctrl/Cmd+K) that jumps you to any of the 50-plus admin pages instantly, filtered to whatever your role is allowed to see.

Admin Pallet

Devtoberfest is warming up

With Devtoberfest coming in October, a wave of seasonal work landed this week as well. The homepage now carries a Devtoberfest banner with a live countdown ticking down to the start. There's a promo video embedded on the Devtoberfest page. The leaderboard got it's final pieces finished, too. Puzzle and Petoberfest completions now autoscore, getting us fully ready for the contest start.

The session experience got a lot more usable. Sessions now carry a Live vs Prerecorded badge with a matching Format filter across the grid, calendar, and schedule views, so you can zero in on the ones you can actually attend live. That was suggestion from a community member which we directly implemented. So if you have ideas, be sure to share them.

Live vs. Prerecorded Tags

Session abstracts render proper Markdown now (headings, lists, links, inline code) instead of collapsing into one run-on paragraph. Speaker names show up right on the calendar items rather than hiding in the popup. And both the calendar and the sessions grid are fully deep-linkable: you can share a URL that lands someone on a specific day, a specific filter, or an open session panel. For example the calendar takes ?view=day&date=2026-10-05&session=<id>&track=<name>, and the sessions grid takes ?q=<text>&week=<w>&track=<name>&session=<id>. And browser back/forward behaves exactly the way you'd hope.

The Selfie boothgot a refresh for the season, with new key-visual and speaker backdrops, new stickers (including "I love ABAP" and a Devtoberfest badge), a no-frame option, and 13 new advocate cut-out frames so you can pose your selfie next to the likes of Kasimir and the developer advocates.

Devtobefest Selfies

And the event displays are no longer stuck saying "TechEd". The /event-display and /app-space screens now show each event's real name, description, and logo, which event admins can upload themselves right from the admin console. This is so we can reuse the tried-and-true Developer Garage infrastructure at SAP Connect and Sapphire moving forward.

Your progress, and a few finishing touches

If you're signed in, the My Completions page now shows tutorials you've started but not finished right alongside the ones you've completed (another community suggestion). Partials show up in the Recent Activity timeline with a play icon and an "In progress · N%" label; click one and it drops you back exactly where you left off. It's a small thing that makes picking a learning session back up much less annoying.

Partial Completions - Easy to Resume

A handful of smaller polish items round it out. Group and mission tag chips now show correct casing, "SAP BTP Cockpit" and "OData" instead of "Sap Btp Cockpit" and "Odata", matching the individual tutorial pages. The homepage's "Explore topic clusters" band got much richer, surfacing the full range of knowledge-graph-connected content (missions, learning journeys, API docs, samples, help docs, blog posts, videos, community events) rather than just tutorials, each with its own type badge and NEW markers. We also finally put a recurring gremlin to rest where curated homepage shelf links kept disappearing after deploys. They now self-heal on every restart, so those shelves stay reliably populated.

Connecting your AI tools over MCP now with proper sign-in

We finished the work that lets you point an AI assistant at developers.sap.com over MCP (the Model Context Protocol) and have it sign in as you. The site now publishes a complete set of discovery endpoints: the .well-known documents that an MCP client reads to figure out where to authenticate. And, crucially, those are now reachable on the live site (we cleared up the CDN rule that had been blocking them). The trickiest part was that our identity provider hands back an HTML login page where MCP clients expect a machine-readable config, which used to make clients choke; the site now advertises itself as the authorization server and quietly forwards the actual sign-in to SAP's universal ID, so the handshake just works.

For you that means a real OAuth 2.1 sign-in with a browser consent step, after which the assistant can call the authenticated tools on your behalf, pulling your in-progress and completed tutorials, your missions and events, marking a step complete, or fetching recommendations tuned to what you've already done. There's also a set of anonymous, read-only tools (search, homepage, knowledge-graph lookups) you can wire up without signing in at all.

To make all of this approachable, there's a new MCP Quickstart in the Help documentation that walks through connecting the common clients: Claude Desktop, Claude Code, and Joule Work Desktop, all with copy-paste config, the correct client ID for the environment you're on, and a personal-access-token route if you'd rather skip the browser flow. If you've been curious about driving your SAP learning from inside your AI assistant, this is the on ramp.

For authors: real reporting back in the admin console

Authors new reporting tools, right inside the admin console. There's a new Reporting folder in the admin navigation with three reports, each of which authors can filter down by mission, group, or individual tutorial (with proper value-help pickers, so you're choosing from a list rather than typing raw names).

Tutorial Engagement is the one most people will live in: it shows, per tutorial, how many people started versus completed it, the count of distinct learners, and the resulting completion rate. A tutorial with lots of starts but a low completion rate jumps out as something that may have a broken quiz or a confusing step. Tutorial Completions plots completion events over time, charted by day, so you can see when interest in a piece of content spiked or tailed off. And Tutorial Survey renders the learner feedback for a mission or group as a set of clean histograms. one per survey question, scored 0 to 10, with the response count and average called out, followed by the free-text comments, with sensible "no responses yet" states when there's nothing to show.

Alongside the standalone reports, the Tutorials admin object page grew a whole set of reporting panels so you can understand a single tutorial at a glance: its Contributors (pulled from git history, linked to their GitHub profiles), its assigned Categories, a Media panel listing every image and asset with its source link and file size, a Freshness panel with the history of automated freshness runs (when it ran, the model used, and how many high-priority issues it flagged), and a Knowledge Graph group showing the concepts a tutorial teaches, the "learners who finished this also finished…" co-completions, its PageRank score, and which community cluster it belongs to. There's also a polished Devtoberfest Signups report with a running-total column, a total-registrations KPI card, and breakdowns by region, edition, and role.

entry.title: September 15th: What's New on developers.sap.com
entry.content:
The theme this stretch is hard to miss: we spent it focused on the platform as something an AI agent can use extensively. Over the last week we closed gaps around agentic consumption and then kept going. Here's the tour.

Every tutorial now has a Markdown twin. Take any tutorial and add .md to the URL, developers.sap.com/tutorials/<slug>.md, and instead of the styled HTML page you get the clean, normalized Markdown source straight from the database, with the slug and canonical URL already stitched into the frontmatter. If you'd rather not rewrite URLs, content negotiation does the same thing on the primary URL: curl -H "Accept: text/markdown" https://developers.sap.com/tutorials/<slug> hands back Markdown, while a normal browser (which never asks for Markdown) still gets the full HTML page. This is the difference between copy-pasting a rendered tutorial into your editor and just pulling it, perfect for feeding a tutorial into Claude, Cursor, or your own tooling without the page furniture getting in the way. Overtime as agents read the tutorial content for you directly, this pays off in a more token efficient option.

 

 

We've added to the hosted MCP server, and it's more discoverable. We publish a manifest at developers.sap.com/.well-known/mcp.json that advertises the anonymous search tier at /mcp/search. Point an MCP client at it and you get curated tools rather than a raw database query hole: search_tutorials, get_tutorial_step, search_events, and a brand-new search_channels that also exposes the new external-channels catalog (search by name, category, or platform like YouTube/Blog/Podcast) to agents.

 

 

The step tool got a nice upgrade too: get_tutorial_step now takes a format argument and defaults to markdown, so an agent can ask for step 3 of a tutorial as Markdown and never pay the token cost of rendering HTML it's going to throw away. The MCP surfaces also now show up properly in the ORD catalog alongside the OData, REST, and GraphQL APIs, so service discovery tools see the full picture.

Semantic search went public. Search across the whole tutorial and concept body now understands meaning, not just keyword. Ask for something like "connect a CAP service to HANA Cloud" and it finds the right material even when the wording doesn't match. The contract is deliberately safe: you send text, the server does the embedding, and you get back scored links to real content: never raw vectors, and it never accepts a vector from the caller. It's exposed both as a public function and as an MCP tool. For example: https://developers.sap.com/search/semantic_search(query='how%20to%20deploy%20a%20CAP%20app',corpus='tutorials',topK=5,minScore=0.25)

 

 

Two new navigation surfaces for humans and machines. There's now a navigable developers.sap.com/sitemap.md that lays out the site's actual structure: the six verb lanes, every mission expanded into its ordered list of tutorials, the top topics, and reference links. That's distinct from the flat sitemap.xml (a crawler's URL list) and the llms.txt / llms-full.txt metadata dumps, both of which also got fixed this week so the "Featured Missions" section actually populates and every tutorial entry points at its .md variant. Together they give an AI tool three complementary ways in: a flat crawl list, a full metadata dump, and a human-readable map of how it all fits together.

You can turn a tutorial into a runnable, verifiable AI Skill. This is the fun one. Hit developers.sap.com/content/tutorials/hana-cloud-cap-create-ui/skill and you get back a zip bundle containing a SKILL.md (the tutorial procedure, stamped with freshness/provenance and a source-commit) plus a generated verify.sh. This is a real bash script built from the tutorial's own assertion blocks (command checks, HTTP checks, file checks), with every value shell-quoted so it's injection-safe. In other words: a tutorial an assistant can install as a Skill and run to check whether the steps still actually work. It builds on two other things that landed alongside it: assertion blocks in tutorial source are now parsed and persisted, and served tutorials can carry a signed Ed25519 provenance envelope (/content/tutorials/<slug>/provenance, with public keys at /.well-known/tutorial-provenance/jwks.json) so a consumer can cryptographically verify where the content came from and how fresh it is. These built in tutorial checks that generate the verify.sh is brand new functionality so very tutorials will have them, but it's a foundation for the future.

Agent-to-agent, documented. The A2A (Agent2Agent) endpoint has been a real first-party surface for a while. We had public Agent Card at developers.sap.com/.well-known/agent-card.json, JSON-RPC over POST /a2a, five skills, but it was only discoverable if you already knew to look in .well-known. Now the developers.sap.com/api-docs/ landing page describes it properly next to the MCP server, and there's a full A2A quickstart with message/send, streaming, and tasks/get examples plus the error-code table.

 

 

The GraphQL docs are expanded now as well. The public GraphQL docs at developers.sap.com/api-docs/graphql/ used to ship examples that every one of them failed. They all queried a value {} wrapper that doesn't exist (it's nodes {} and totalCount) and a made-up search argument. All five examples were rewritten and verified live, and the advertised SDL is finally served: developers.sap.com/graphql/schema.graphql returns the full ~100KB schema so you can point codegen or a client straight at it.

A little something for fun but also helpful to new developers in our ecosystem: Kasimir Teaches TLAs. SAP runs on three- and four-letter acronyms, so we built a tongue-in-cheek, Duolingo-style trainer for them at developers.sap.com/explore/ktt/, narrated by an animated Professor Kasimir the cat. It launched with 4 units / 12 lessons / 48 acronyms and grew over the weekend to 5 units / 14 lessons / 58 acronyms, including ABAP and BDC (SAP Business Data Cloud) slotted next to RAP and DWC, and a whole new "SAP & AI" unit covering the essentials (AI, ML, LLM, RAG) and SAP's own stack (BAIP, NLP, ISLM, MCP). It also got real progress tracking this weekend: mastering a lesson now requires a genuine 70% pass. Get everything wrong and you land on a "you need 70% to master this" screen with a Try Again button instead of a "Kasimir approves 🐱". And your XP finally shows up, with level tiers that climb from Kitten to Curious Cat to Clever Cat to Acronym Adept to TLA Sage, plus a streak counter. If people enjoy this feature and let us know we will add more like this in the future.

 

 

Smarter guidance. A new prerequisite-chain reasoner can look at the knowledge graph and answer "what should I learn next" three ways: the path to a specific tutorial, the path to finish a whole mission or group, or just a next-best suggestion when you have no particular goal. It shows up as a "Your Learning Path" panel on tutorial and mission pages and as an MCP tool, and it personalizes against what you've already completed. That personalization happens at request time and is never stored, so your history stays your own.

 

 

Quality-of-life across authoring and content. Admins got a one-click Copy Mission in the Missions list. They select a mission, hit Copy, and the backend deep-copies the whole graph (the mission, its completion paths and items, its tag and category links) into a fresh unpublished mission named <slug>-copy, then drops you into the new object page; referenced tutorials and tags are linked, not cloned. Authors can now build a personal watch list in the Tutorial Health dashboard to monitor tutorials they don't own, with the report scoped to owned, watching, or both. Tutorial owners started getting a daily email digest of new commented feedback (rating-only submissions don't spam them) so we can react to your feedback faster.

On the content side: tutorial images now use absolute URLs so they load wherever they're embedded, event descriptions render Markdown as clean safe HTML, Devtoberfest session pages link to their feedback surveys, and the tag taxonomy now syncs itself weekly against the central Semaphore model so renamed terms update in place.

And a lot of keeping-the-lights-on. Under the hood we added a WAF-style input-validation layer on the anonymous/agent write surface plus depth-and-complexity limits (and a production introspection block) on the public GraphQL endpoint; a shared, cross-instance rate limiter; an Akamai edge-cache fast-purge hook so freshly published content reaches you sooner instead of hammering the database on every request; and a load-shedding guard that returns a polite 503 with Retry-After under sudden spikes rather than falling over. Concept pages also build faster now by reading their link tables in parallel. Most of this is invisible when it's working, which is the whole idea.

It's hard to believe but it's only one week before Devtoberfest, so updates on developers.sap.com might slow as we are busy with Devtoberfest, TechEd, and TechEd on Tour. However, you can always view the backlog or submit your own ideas for the future.

entry.title: Agentic UI Extensibility: The Next Chapter of SAPUI5 Flexibility
entry.content:
For over a decade, SAPUI5 Flexibility has let end users, key users, and developers adapt SAP Fiori apps without modifying the underlying code. Moving fields, adding tables, creating app variants, and personalizing views are all persisted as layered changes. It's the technology that makes Clean Core extensibility on the UI possible.

This session opens the next chapter. We'll unveil agentic UI extensibility and walk through what's new across the SAPUI5 Flexibility stack: a redesigned UX for key user adaptation, real performance gains, and expanded BTP Cloud Foundry support. We'll also show where it's all heading: unified and agentic UI extensibility. Starting as a key user using Joule, then transitioning into a more advanced developer scenario using MCP servers to create and extend SAPUI5 adaptation projects, including taking over existing key user changes. The same trusted foundation (layers, change handlers, stable IDs) becomes the safe, governed action layer that agents build on, so AI-generated adaptations stay upgrade-safe, transportable, and reversible.
